name: Roxbury
headline: A puddingstone hill with an 1869 standpipe tower,
row houses and triple-deckers around Nubian Square.
answer: Roxbury is a Boston neighborhood that the city's planning department describes as the geographic heart of Boston, settled in 1630 and annexed to Boston in 1868. Its housing runs from Greek Revival and Italianate houses on Fort Hill to brick row houses and triple-deckers, and the Boston Planning & Development Agency counted 54,905 people there in 2020. The Silver Line runs on Washington Street from Nubian Square, and the Orange Line and commuter rail stop at Ruggles.
meta: Roxbury, Boston: Fort Hill's Greek Revival houses, row houses and triple-deckers around Nubian Square, with the Silver Line, the Orange Line and Franklin Park.

boundaries.text: Roxbury sits at the center of Boston: Columbia Road separates it from Dorchester, Franklin Park is divided between Roxbury and Jamaica Plain along Walnut Avenue and Sigourney Street, and Ruggles station stands where Roxbury, the Fenway and Mission Hill meet. Melnea Cass Boulevard runs roughly over the line of the old Roxbury Canal.

overview: Roxbury was settled on September 28, 1630, and its First Church was gathered in 1632. William Pynchon, one of the founders, left in 1636 with a group of the town's men to found Springfield. The town's houses were set on Roxbury puddingstone, a conglomerate quarried for foundations. Several 18th-century buildings survive: Governor William Shirley built the Shirley-Eustis House as a summer house between 1747 and 1751, and the Dillaway-Thomas House, a parsonage begun in 1750, served as a Continental Army headquarters during the Siege of Boston in 1775. Roxbury became a city in 1846, part of it was set off as the town of West Roxbury in 1851, and Boston annexed the rest on January 5, 1868.

Row houses and multi-family buildings followed trolley service, which began in 1887, and the Washington Street Elevated reached Dudley Square, now Nubian Square, on June 10, 1901. The building stock shows each period. On Fort Hill, around Highland Park, Greek Revival and Italianate houses that predate the Civil War stand among triple-deckers and row houses, below an 1869 standpipe tower built for Roxbury's water system. The Moreland Street district was built up between about 1840 and 1920 with Second Empire, Italianate and Queen Anne houses, and in Lower Roxbury the Tremont Improvement Company built row houses on filled salt marsh around what became Frederick Douglass Square in 1917.

The last train ran on the Washington Street Elevated on April 30, 1987, and the Orange Line moved to the Southwest Corridor, with new stations at Ruggles and Roxbury Crossing opening on May 4. Silver Line buses began running on Washington Street on July 20, 2002. The Boston Planning & Development Agency started PLAN: Dudley Square in 2016 to guide public and vacant parcels around the square, and its board approved the plan's development guidelines on July 11, 2019. On December 19, 2019, the city's Public Improvement Commission renamed Dudley Square as Nubian Square, and in 2022 the city designated the Highland Park Architectural Conservation District, about 170 acres of steep, puddingstone-studded land also called Roxbury Highlands or Fort Hill.

housing.text: The Boston Planning Department describes Roxbury's housing as historic brick row houses and Boston's traditional triple-deckers; Fort Hill adds Greek Revival, Italianate and later Victorian houses, and Cedar Street has a run of 1871 Second Empire row houses. The Boston Planning & Development Agency's tabulation of the 2016-2020 American Community Survey counts 20,681 occupied housing units in Roxbury, 26.1% of them owner-occupied, compared with 35.3% citywide.

areas.name: Nubian Square
areas.line: The commercial center formerly called Dudley Square, framed by Washington Street, Malcolm X Boulevard, Dudley Street and Guild Row, with Nubian station, the Silver Line terminus and a large MBTA bus terminal, and the Ferdinand Building, now Boston Public Schools headquarters.

areas.name: Fort Hill (Highland Park)
areas.line: A 0.4-square-mile hill bounded by Malcolm X Boulevard, Washington Street and Columbus Avenue, named for a Revolutionary War earthwork; listed on the National Register as the Roxbury Highlands Historic District on February 22, 1989, it holds Greek Revival and Italianate houses, triple-deckers and row houses, and John Eliot Square with the First Church and the Dillaway-Thomas House.

areas.name: Moreland Street Historic District
areas.line: A 63-acre, mainly residential district roughly bounded by Kearsarge and Blue Hill Avenues and Warren, Waverly and Winthrop Streets, developed between about 1840 and 1920 and listed on the National Register on March 29, 1984.

areas.name: Frederick Douglass Square
areas.line: Lower Roxbury row houses in Second Empire, Queen Anne and Gothic styles, built on filled salt marsh between Hammond, Cabot, Windsor and Westminster Streets; the district was listed on the National Register on October 3, 1996.

rail.line: Commuter rail (Providence/Stoughton, Franklin/Foxboro and Needham Lines)
Silver Line SL4 and SL5 (bus rapid transit)

commute.text: The Silver Line runs on Washington Street from Nubian station, the SL4 to South Station and the SL5 to Downtown Crossing, following the route of the elevated line that closed in 1987. The Orange Line stops at Ruggles, on Tremont Street, and at Roxbury Crossing, at Tremont Street and Columbus Avenue, on the neighborhood's western side; Ruggles is also a stop on the Providence/Stoughton, Franklin/Foxboro and Needham commuter rail lines, though some trains pass it. Washington Street, Blue Hill Avenue, Columbus Avenue and Melnea Cass Boulevard are the main roads.

places.name: Franklin Park
places.line: Olmsted's park of roughly 485 acres, designed in the 1890s and Boston's largest open space, with the Franklin Park Zoo, the William Devine Golf Course and White Stadium; it connects Roxbury with Dorchester, Jamaica Plain, Mattapan and Roslindale.

places.name: Franklin Park Zoo
places.line: A 72-acre zoo in the northeast part of Franklin Park, opened on October 4, 1912 and run by Zoo New England, with a 3-acre Tropical Forest building under a fabric dome.

places.name: Roxbury Heritage State Park
places.line: A state park at 183 Roxbury Street in John Eliot Square, built around the Dillaway-Thomas House of about 1750, now a museum, with landscaped grounds looking toward the Boston skyline.

places.name: Shirley-Eustis House
places.line: Governor William Shirley's summer house at 33 Shirley Street, built between 1747 and 1751 and later owned by Governor William Eustis; a National Historic Landmark since October 9, 1960, open to the public since 1991.

places.name: Highland Park and the Cochituate Standpipe
places.line: The park on the summit of Fort Hill, landscaped by Frederick Law Olmsted, with a Victorian tower designed by Nathaniel J. Bradlee around the standpipe Roxbury built in 1869 for its water system.

places.name: First Church in Roxbury
places.line: The congregation's meetinghouse at Highland Avenue and Centre Street in John Eliot Square, described as Boston's oldest surviving wooden meeting house of the Federal period.

places.name: Malcolm X-Ella Little-Collins House
places.line: A Victorian house at 72 Dale Street, one of a row built on the former Abijah Seaver estate, designated a Boston Landmark in 1998 and surveyed by city archaeologists in 2016.

history.text: Roxbury was settled on September 28, and its First Church was gathered two years later.
Boston annexed the city of Roxbury on January 5.
The Washington Street Elevated opened on June 10, running as far as Dudley Square.
The elevated line closed on April 30, and the Orange Line reopened on May 4 in the Southwest Corridor, with new stations at Ruggles and Roxbury Crossing.
On December 19 the Public Improvement Commission renamed Dudley Square as Nubian Square, following a November 5 advisory ballot question.

faq.q: What is the median home price in Roxbury?
faq.a: According to The Warren Group's MA December 2025 Sales, Prices by Town table, which lists Roxbury on its own row, the median single-family sale price for calendar year 2025 was $712,000, across 20 sales, against $654,125 across 24 sales in 2024. The condominium median was $618,000 in 2025, across 117 sales, against $600,000 across 149 sales in 2024. Much of Roxbury's housing is row houses and multi-family buildings, which the single-family figure does not cover.

faq.q: Why is Dudley Square now called Nubian Square?
faq.a: After a non-binding advisory question on the November 5, 2019 ballot, the city's Public Improvement Commission approved the change on December 19, 2019, and the MBTA's bus station there is now Nubian station. The new name refers to Nubia, a region in present-day Egypt and Sudan; the old one honored Thomas Dudley, a governor of the Massachusetts Bay Colony.

notes: Written 2026-10-23. Population: Boston Planning & Development Agency Research Division, 'Boston in Context: Neighborhoods' (April 2022), 'Population by Age Group' table, row 'Roxbury 54,905 ...' (2020 Census, neighborhoods approximated with 2020 block groups; Mission Hill and the Fenway are separate neighborhoods in that report). Housing tenure from the same report's Housing Tenure table (ACS 2016-2020): 'Roxbury 20,681 92.1% 5,396 26.1% 15,285 73.9%'; Boston 35.3%. The report has no units-in-structure, year-built or land-area tables, so no housing-type shares or acreage are given. Housing types: Boston Planning Department neighborhood page (https://www.bostonplans.org/neighborhoods/roxbury: 'historic brick row houses and Boston's traditional triple-deckers'; 'the geographic heart of Boston, enclosing the center point of the city'); Fort Hill styles from Wikipedia's Roxbury Highlands Historic District article; Cedar Street 1871 row houses and 1887 trolley from Wikipedia's Roxbury article. Highland Park Architectural Conservation District: designated 2022, about 170 acres, also called Roxbury Highlands or Fort Hill, annexed 1868 (https://www.boston.gov/historic-district/highland-park-architectural-conservation-district); its boundaries and exact designation date were not on the page. The Roxbury Highlands National Register district is given as 0.4 square miles on Wikipedia; the city's 170 acres is for the conservation district, a different boundary; both are reported as their sources give them. First Church: Wikipedia gives the current building as 1803 (Roxbury Highlands article) and 1804 (Roxbury article), so no year is used. Standpipe: built 1869 per Wikipedia; the tower's designer (Bradlee) is from the same article; the tower's own date was not confirmed. Annexation January 5, 1868 and 1846 city, 1851 West Roxbury from the Roxbury Wikipedia infobox and footnote. Pynchon leaving in 1636 for Springfield: Wikipedia. Dillaway-Thomas House: mass.gov (about 1750, 1775 headquarters); Wikipedia's John Eliot Square article says 1750 as a parsonage. Nubian Square: Wikipedia (bounds, Dudley namesake, Nubia, Nubian station renamed mid-February 2020) and Boston.com (December 19, 2019 commission vote, November 5, 2019 advisory question, street-register change). PLAN: Dudley Square/Nubian Square dates from https://www.bostonplans.org/planning/planning-initiatives/plan-nubian-square. Ferdinand Building as Boston Public Schools headquarters is from the Planning Department's neighborhood page (the Bolling Building Wikipedia page would not load, so its opening date is not given). Transit: Ruggles (1150 Tremont St, Roxbury) from mbta.com; Ruggles on the Providence/Stoughton, Franklin/Foxboro and Needham timetables on mbta.com (some trips skip it); Ruggles and Roxbury Crossing openings May 4, 1987 and the elevated's last run April 30, 1987 from their Wikipedia articles; Wikipedia places Roxbury Crossing station in Mission Hill and Ruggles where Roxbury, Fenway-Kenmore and Mission Hill meet, so both are described as on the western side rather than inside Roxbury. Jackson Square station is listed under Jamaica Plain and is not repeated here. Silver Line SL4/SL5 routes, July 20, 2002 start and October 13, 2009 SL4/SL5 designations from Wikipedia's Silver Line article; the mbta.com SL5 and Nubian stop pages did not list routes. Main roads are named from the Nubian Square, Ruggles, Roxbury Crossing and Roxbury articles and the Planning Department page; route numbers were not confirmed and are not given. Malcolm X-Ella Little-Collins House: city archaeology page (72 Dale Street, Boston Landmark 1998, 2016 survey); the page gives conflicting build dates (1874; between 1845 and 1866), so none is used, and the National Register listing date was not given. Left out: Eliot Burying Ground (founding date only from Wikipedia's list, not cross-checked), the Planning Department's '570 acres of parks' figure (it may count Franklin Park, which is shared), the Roxbury Strategic Master Plan (2004 document date only; adoption date not on the page), and the Boston Water and Sewer Commission lot housing plan (planned, not built). Market: both rows copied from tools/data/boston-neighborhood-rows-2025.json (read 2026-10-23 with pdf.js; YTD lines are calendar years 2024 and 2025); the PDF was not re-read here. Schools: assignment is by address and set by Boston Public Schools; no school is named (the Planning Department page names a high school, not used). Nearby: Roxbury borders Dorchester and Jamaica Plain (Wikipedia), and Franklin Park connects it with Mattapan (city park page); the South End is included as a neighboring slug, but a source naming it as a border was not opened in this session. Mission Hill and the Fenway are not in the slug list. Region: kept as 'Greater Boston (the city)' to match the eight existing Boston neighborhood records. Fair housing: the Planning Department page and Wikipedia's Roxbury article both describe migration and the population by group, and Wikipedia describes Fort Hill as gentrified; none of this is used, even as history. The Nubian Square renaming is told through the ballot question, the commission vote and the place-name meanings only, without describing who supported it or who voted. The Malcolm X-Ella Little-Collins House is named as a Boston Landmark at its address, with no description of its occupants beyond the building's name. No section is characterized by who lives there, and no crime or safety language is used.
